claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure containing distinct nanoscale and microscale phases and interfaces.
A machine-learning surrogate integrating hierarchical microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior for HfNbTiVAl10.
The surrogate's property predictions will have approximately 10% or lower error relative to experiments and full-scale simulations.
The surrogate will use less than 20% of the computational time, corresponding to at least an 80% resource reduction relative to established simulations.
The surrogate can be trained using grain size, phase distribution, interphase-interface characteristics, and limited ab initio and mesoscale simulation data.
The hierarchical structure is stable and well defined during room-temperature tensile and fracture tests at controlled strain rates.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates load transfer through its phase boundaries and interfaces.
The phase boundaries and interfaces regulate dislocation mobility and thereby govern elastic and plastic responses.
The surrogate will learn scaling relationships between microstructural features and mechanical properties across multiple length scales.
Learning these multiscale relationships will enable rapid property estimation with reduced simulation complexity.
Conventional molecular-dynamics or continuum finite-element approaches require extensive multiscale analysis and longer computational times.
Predictive performance may fail when the hierarchical structure is insufficiently characterized.
Predictive performance may fail under unrepresented phase transformations or microstructural evolution, including at extreme temperatures or strain rates.
Prediction error and resource savings depend on the quality and coverage of the training dataset.
Extrapolation outside the training regime is uncertain.
A prediction deviation greater than 15% from experimental and full-scale simulation results is predeclared to falsify the hypothesis.
Computational time savings below 80% relative to conventional methods are predeclared to falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction target is approximately 10% error, whereas the falsification rule requires error greater than 15%. Thus, an error between 10% and 15% would fail the stated performance target without satisfying the declared falsification criterion.
